newsitem.title: USA: Judge allows Simpson to claim evidence was planted.
newsitem.headline: Judge allows Simpson to claim evidence was planted.

text.p: The judge in O.J. Simpson's civil trial ruled on Friday that the former football star's lawyers may tell the jury their theory that evidence was planted in an attempt to frame him for murder.

The decision by Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki was a victory for Simpson, allowing his lawyers to argue in opening statements that former Los Angeles police detective Mark Fuhrman planted a bloody glove on Simpson's estate the morning after his ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend, Ronald Goldman, were slashed to death.

Fuhrman, who last week pleaded no contest to perjury arising out of his testimony during Simpson's criminal case, was painted by defence attorneys at that trial as a racist and a rogue cop. He has since retired and lives in Idaho.
Simpson was acquitted last October of the June 12, 1994, murders and is now fighting a civil wrongful-death civil case brought by the victims' families.

At a brief court hearing on Friday, Fujisaki ruled that Simpson's defence team could also present theories that blood was planted on the rear gate of Nicole Simpson's townhouse, in Simpson's white Ford Bronco and on socks found in his mansion.

The defence in the criminal trial depicted Simpson as the victim of a broad police conspiracy, but prosecutors contended there was no evidence of a frame-up. In his ruling on Friday, Fujisaki said evidence regarding the bloody glove found at Simpson's house was "very slim to support a planting theory."

"However, inasmuch as a principal witness (Fuhrman) has pleaded nolo contendre (no contest) to perjury ... that is a sufficient basis on which to make an argument" that the glove was planted, he added.
Fuhrman's plea, the equivalent of an admission of guilt, did not relate to his finding the glove but to his denial at the trial that he had used racial slurs in the past 10 years.
Blood on the glove matched that of Simpson, his ex-wife and Goldman.

With regard to traces of blood found in Simpson's car, Fujisaki said the defence could make a planting argument only with regard to stains found some two months after the murders, and not for blood found during the initial search the day the bodies were discovered. Experts at Simpson's criminal trial testified that blood found on both occasions matched samples from Simpson and the two victims.

But Fujisaki denied Simpson's lawyers the right to argue a planting theory about a glove and knit cap found at the crime scene or the bulk of the bloodstains found on June 13, both at the crime scene and at Simpson's home. He also decided that a visit by jurors to the crime scene in the upscale area of Brentwood and to Simpson's home nearby would serve no purpose.

Fujisaki made it clear that Simpson's defence team could raise their planting theory when questioning their own witnesses and cross-examining the plaintiffs' witnesses but he warned: "I don't want a bunch of grand theories placed before a jury where ... there is no basis for these theories."

The third and final phase of jury selection, in which prospective panel members will face a wide range of questions from lawyers, begins on Tuesday. A total of 102 possible jurors remain after others were excused because of hardship or because of their views based on the first trial and subsequent publicity.
